fields.title: A Catena on the Psalms
fields.subtitle: The Psalms, verse by verse, with the Church’s great commentators
fields.description: All hundred and fifty Psalms, read slowly, the way the Church has prayed them for centuries: under each verse, the great commentators speak one after another, oldest first. Augustine preaching on the Psalms in Hippo, John Calvin in Geneva, the Jesuit cardinal Robert Bellarmine, Matthew Henry, the Hebrew scholar Franz Delitzsch, A. R. Fausset, and C. H. Spurgeon, whose Treasury of David is the voice heard most often, each quoted word for word from a public-domain edition. The Psalms themselves are the Open Word Bible, a new translation given freely to the public domain. A catena (Latin for “chain”) is one of the oldest ways of studying Scripture; this one gives a chapter to each psalm, a psalm a day, with an introduction on how to read it and a closing chapter on the voices and their books.

qa.question: What is a catena on the Psalms?
qa.answer: A catena, from the Latin for “chain”, is a commentary built from other commentaries: under each verse of Scripture, excerpts from earlier interpreters are linked one after another, so the reader hears several voices on the same words. This one does that for the whole Book of Psalms, from Psalm 1 to Psalm 150.

qa.question: Whose commentary is in this catena on the Psalms?
qa.answer: Seven commentators, from the early Church to the late 1800s: Augustine, John Calvin, Robert Bellarmine, Matthew Henry, Franz Delitzsch, A. R. Fausset and C. H. Spurgeon. Spurgeon’s Treasury of David is quoted most often. Every excerpt is copied word for word from a public-domain English edition, as gathered by the open collection Logia.

qa.question: Which Bible translation does this catena use?
qa.answer: The text of the Psalms is the Open Word Bible, English, Balanced level, a new translation dedicated to the public domain. Inside the excerpts, the commentators quote the Psalms in the English of their own editions: usually the King James Version, though Augustine and Bellarmine read the Psalms in Latin and their translators rendered that.

qa.question: How is this catena arranged?
qa.answer: One chapter for each psalm, in order. Within a chapter the psalm comes first, a verse or a few verses at a time, followed by the commentators who wrote on those words, in the order they lived. Every verse of the Psalms appears once, in order, so the book can also be read straight through as the Psalter.

qa.question: Why do some commentators number the psalms or verses differently?
qa.answer: In the Hebrew Bible a psalm’s title often counts as its first verse, so Delitzsch, who worked from the Hebrew, often numbers a verse one higher than English Bibles do. Augustine and Bellarmine read a Latin Bible that joins Psalms 9 and 10, so most of their psalm numbers are one lower: their Psalm 22 is the English Psalm 23. This book uses the English numbers throughout and places every excerpt under the verse it discusses.

qa.question: Is every word of the commentators included?
qa.answer: No. Between them the seven commentators wrote millions of words on the Psalms. This catena is a selection, chosen so that each psalm is heard from more than one century and more than one tradition. Each excerpt is given whole, in the words of its edition.

qa.question: Do the commentators agree with one another?
qa.answer: Not always. Augustine hears Christ and his Church in nearly every psalm, Calvin looks first for David’s own meaning, Bellarmine reads as a Catholic where Calvin, Henry and Spurgeon read as Protestants, and Delitzsch weighs the Hebrew more closely than anyone. A catena keeps these differences side by side.

qa.question: How should I read a catena on the Psalms?
qa.answer: Slowly. A psalm a day takes you through the Psalter in five months, and the longest, Psalm 119, can be spread over several days. Read the psalm first, then the voices beneath it, then the psalm again as a prayer.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The Psalms have been the Church’s prayer book from the beginning. Monks sang all hundred and fifty of them every week; reformers set them to metre so whole congregations could sing them; preachers have opened them to the sick, the dying and the glad for two thousand years. And because so many have prayed them, so many have written on them. This book gathers some of that writing in the old way, as a catena, a chain: under each verse, the words of earlier readers linked one after another, so that a single line of a psalm comes with a whole conversation attached.

How this book works

Each chapter of the book is one psalm, from the first to the hundred and fiftieth, under the heading the Open Word Bible gives it. The psalm comes first, a verse or a few verses at a time, set apart as a quotation. Then come the commentators who wrote on those words, in the order they lived: the early Church first, then the Reformation, then the eighteenth century, then the nineteenth. Then the psalm moves on. Every verse of the Psalms appears once, in order, so the book can be read straight through as the Psalter itself.

You will not find every commentator on every verse. Between them these writers left millions of words on the Psalms, far more than anyone could read in a year. What is here is a selection, chosen so that each psalm is heard from more than one century and more than one tradition. A short psalm gets a few voices; a long one gets more, though never as many as its verses. Where a verse has no comment beneath it, the psalm simply speaks for itself.

The voices

There are seven of them. From the early Church comes Augustine, who preached and wrote on every one of the Psalms. From the Reformation come John Calvin in Geneva and the Jesuit cardinal Robert Bellarmine, a Protestant and a Catholic reading the same psalms within a lifetime of each other. From the 1700s comes Matthew Henry, whose commentary has fed English-speaking Christians for three hundred years. From the 1800s come the German Hebrew scholar Franz Delitzsch, A. R. Fausset of the Church of England, and Charles Haddon Spurgeon, the Baptist preacher of London, whose Treasury of David is the voice heard most often here.

They do not always agree. Augustine hears Christ and his Church in nearly every psalm; Calvin looks first for David’s own meaning; Delitzsch weighs the Hebrew; Spurgeon preaches. That is part of the point. A catena does not hand you one reading and close the book; it lets you overhear the Church praying and thinking aloud, and then sends you back to the psalm. The last chapter of this book says a little more about each of them, and names the edition every excerpt was taken from.

A note on the numbers

This book numbers the psalms and their verses as English Bibles do. Not every commentator did. In the Hebrew Bible a psalm’s title, such as “A psalm of David”, often counts as its first verse, so the verses after it run one number ahead of ours, and Delitzsch, who worked from the Hebrew, numbers them that way: his “ver. 2” is often our verse 1. Augustine and Bellarmine read the Psalms in Latin, in a Bible that counts Psalms 9 and 10 as one, so from there on most of their psalm numbers are one lower than ours: their Psalm 22 is our Psalm 23. None of this changes where an excerpt stands. Each one is placed under the verse it actually discusses, whatever number its author gave it.

A note on the words

The text of the Psalms is the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain. The commentators wrote long before it, and when they quote a psalm they quote the English of their own editions: usually the King James Version, though Augustine’s and Bellarmine’s translators rendered the Latin they read. So you will read “The Lord is my shepherd” in one place and “The Lord feedeth me” in another. Both reach back to the same psalm.

Every excerpt is copied word for word from a public-domain English edition, as gathered by Logia, an open collection of the Church’s commentary. Old spelling and punctuation stand as printed; only the typesetting has been tidied. Several of these editions survive only as old scans, which misread a word here and there, so excerpts the scan had damaged were passed over.

How to read it

Slowly. A psalm a day takes you through the Psalter in five months; the longest, Psalm 119, can be taken over several days. Read the psalm first, then the voices, then the psalm again, this time as a prayer. Notice where the commentators agree and where they part company, and what each one sees that the others miss. The Psalms end where all of this is meant to end: “Let every creature that breathes praise the LORD!”

fields.title: Psalm 1
fields.body_html:
The two ways

How blessed is the one who does not walk by the advice of the wicked, or stand on the path that sinners tread, or sit where mockers gather! Instead, the instruction of the LORD is their delight, and they recite it quietly to themselves day and night. That person is like a tree set out beside channels of water, which bears its fruit when its season comes, and whose leaves never dry up. Whatever they do turns out well.

— Psalm 1:1–3

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

... As to those who bring forth only the leaves of profession, without any good fruit, even their leaf will wither and they shall be as much ashamed of their profession as ever they were proud of it; but, if the word of God rule in the heart, that will keep the profession green, both to our comfort and to our credit; the laurels thus won shall never wither. [5.] That prosperity shall attend him wherever he goes, soul-prosperity. Whatever he does, in conformity to the law, it shall prosper and succeed to his mind, or above his hope.

In singing these verses, being duly affected with the malignant and dangerous nature of sin, the transcendent excellencies of the divine law, and the power and efficacy of God’s grace, from which our fruit is found, we must teach and admonish ourselves, and one another, to watch against sin and all approaches towards it, to converse much with the word of God, and abound in the fruit of righteousness; and, in praying over them, we must seek to God for his grace both to fortify us against every evil word and work and to furnish us for every good word and work.

The wicked are nothing like that. They are like chaff, scattered by the wind. That is why the wicked will not stand firm when judgment comes, and sinners will have no place in the gathering of the righteous.

— Psalm 1:4–5

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

They shall stand there to be judged, but not to be acquitted. Fear shall lay hold upon them there; they shall not stand their ground; they shall flee away; they shall not stand in their own defence; for they shall blush and be covered with eternal contempt.

Well may the saints long for heaven, for no evil men shall dwell there, “nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.” All our congregations upon earth are mixed. Every Church has one devil in it. The tares grow in the same furrows as the wheat. There is no floor which is as yet thoroughly purged from chaff. Sinners mix with saints, as dross mingles with gold. God’s precious diamonds still lie in the same field with pebbles. Righteous Lots are this side heaven continually vexed by the men of Sodom. Let us rejoice then, that in “the general assembly and church of the firstborn” above, there shall by no means be admitted a single unrenewed soul. Sinners cannot live in heaven. They would be out of their element. Sooner could a fish live upon a tree than the wicked in Paradise. Heaven would be an intolerable hell to an impenitent man, even if he could be allowed to enter; but such a privilege shall never be granted to the man who perseveres in his iniquities. May God grant that we may have a name and a place in his courts above!

For the LORD knows the path of the righteous and cares for it, but the path of the wicked ends in ruin.

— Psalm 1:6
fields.summary: The one who delights in God’s instruction is like a tree planted by streams of water, while the wicked are like chaff that the wind blows away. With Matthew Henry and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 2
fields.body_html:
The king the LORD has anointed

Why are the nations in an uproar, and the peoples muttering empty schemes? The kings of the earth take up their positions, and the rulers plot together against the LORD and against his anointed king. “Let us snap their chains,” they say, “and fling their ropes off us.” The one seated on the throne in the heavens laughs; the Lord ridicules them.

— Psalm 2:1–4

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

Let us now turn our eyes from the wicked council-chamber and raging tumult of man, to the secret place of the majesty of the Most High. What doth God say? What will the King do unto the men who reject his only-begotten Son, the Heir of all things?

Mark the quiet dignity of the Omnipotent One, and the contempt which he pours upon the princes and their raging people. He has not taken the trouble to rise up and do battle with them — he despises them, he knows how absurd, how irrational, how futile are their attempts against him — he therefore laughs at them.

Then he speaks to them in anger and fills them with terror in his blazing rage. “I am the one who has set my king in place on Zion, my holy mountain.” I will announce the decree. The LORD said to me, “You are my son. This is the day I have become your father. Ask me, and I will give you the nations to inherit, and the farthest places of the earth to hold as your own.

— Psalm 2:5–8

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

We have heard what the kings of the earth have to say against Christ’s kingdom, and have heard it gainsaid by him that sits in heaven; let us now hear what the Messiah himself has to say for his kingdom, to make good his claims, and it is what all the powers on earth cannot gainsay.

I. The kingdom of the Messiah is founded upon a decree, an eternal decree, of God the Father. It was not a sudden resolve, it was not the trial of an experiment, but the result of the counsels of the divine wisdom and the determinations of the divine will, before all worlds, neither of which can be altered—the precept or statute (so some read it), the covenant or compact (so others), the federal transactions between the Father and the Son concerning man’s redemption, represented by the covenant of royalty made with David and his seed, Ps. lxxxix. 3. This our Lord Jesus often referred to as that which, all along in his undertaking, he governed himself by; This is the will of him that sent me, John vi. 40. This commandment have I received of my Father, John x. 18; xiv. 31.

“You will crush them with an iron scepter and smash them to pieces like a clay pot.”

— Psalm 2:9

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

This is expressly stated to teach us that Christ is furnished with power by which to reign even over those who are averse to his authority, and refuse to obey him. The language of David implies that all will not voluntarily receive his yoke, but that many will be stiff-necked and rebellious, whom notwithstanding he shall subdue by force, and compel to submit to him. It is true, the beauty and glory of the kingdom of which David speaks are more illustriously displayed when a willing people run to Christ in the day of his power, to show themselves his obedient subjects; but as the greater part of men rise up against him with a violence which spurns all restraint, it was necessary to add the truth, that this king would prove himself superior to all such opposition. Of this unconquerable power in war God exhibited a specimen, primarily in the person of David, who, as we know, vanquished and overthrew many enemies by force of arms. But the prediction is more fully verified in Christ, who, neither by sword nor spear, but by the breath of his mouth, smites the ungodly even to their utter destruction.

So then, you kings, show good sense! Accept correction, you who rule the earth. Serve the LORD with awe, and let your joy be mixed with trembling. Kiss the son, or he will be angry and you will come to ruin on your path, for his anger can blaze up in an instant. How blessed are all who make him their refuge!

— Psalm 2:10–12
fields.summary: The nations plot against God and the anointed king, but God laughs at them and declares the king to be God’s son, set on Zion; the rulers are warned to serve God. With John Calvin, Matthew Henry and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 3
fields.body_html:
A shield all around me

LORD, how my enemies have multiplied! Many are rising up against me.

— Psalm 3:1

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

... And it may seem strange, whether in the history of the kings, when Absalom carried on war against his father; or in the history of the New Testament, when Judas was the betrayer of our Lord; how “father’s peace” can be understood. But both in the former place they who read carefully, see that David in that war was at peace with his son, who even with sore grief lamented his death, saying, “O Absalom, my son, would God I had died for thee!” And in the history of the New Testament by that so great and so wonderful forbearance of our Lord; in that He bore so long with him as if good, when He was not ignorant of his thoughts; in that He admitted him to the Supper in which He committed and delivered to His disciples the figure of His Body and Blood; finally, in that He received the kiss of peace at the very time of His betrayal; it is easily understood how Christ showed peace to His betrayer, although he was laid waste by the intestine war of so abominable a device. And therefore is Absalom called “father’s peace,” because his father had the peace, which he had not.

Many are saying about me, “God is not going to rescue him.” Selah But you, LORD, are a shield on every side of me. You are my glory, and you lift my head up again. I lift my voice and call to the LORD, and from his holy mountain he answers me. Selah I lay down and fell asleep, and I woke up again, because the LORD holds me up. I have no fear of the tens of thousands who have taken up positions against me on every side.

— Psalm 3:2–6

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

... “I have not lain,” says he, “waking and restless on my bed; but I have slept soundly, whereas such manner of sleeping does not generally happen to those who are full of thought and fear.” But let us particularly notice that David came to have this confidence of safety from the protection of God, and not from stupidity of mind. Even the wicked are kept fast asleep through an intoxication of mind, while they dream of having made a covenant with death. It was otherwise with David, who found rest on no other ground but because he was upheld by the power of God, and defended by his help. In the next verse, he enlarges upon the incalculable efficacy of this confidence, of which all the godly have some understanding, from their experience of the divine protection. As the power of God is infinite, so they conclude that it shall be invincible against all the assaults, outrages, preparations, and forces of the whole world. And, indeed, unless we ascribe this honor to God, our courage shall be always failing us. Let us, therefore, learn, when in dangers, not to measure the assistance of God after the manner of man, but to despise whatever terrors may stand in our way, inasmuch as all the attempts which men may make against God, are of little or no account.

Rise up, LORD! Rescue me, my God! For you have struck all my enemies across the jaw and smashed the teeth of the wicked. It is the LORD who saves. Let your blessing rest on your people. Selah

— Psalm 3:7–8
fields.summary: David, fleeing from Absalom, cries out that his enemies are many, yet he lies down and sleeps, for God is his shield and rescue. With Augustine and John Calvin.

fields.title: Psalm 4
fields.body_html:
Lying down in peace

When I call, answer me, God who stands up for my right! When I was hemmed in, you gave me room. Show me grace now and listen to my prayer.

— Psalm 4:1

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

This is another instance of David’s common habit of pleading past mercies as a ground for present favour. Here he reviews his Ebenezers and takes comfort from them. It is not to be imagined that he who has helped us in six troubles will leave us in the seventh. God does nothing by halves, and he will never cease to help us until we cease to need. The manna shall fall every morning until we cross the Jordan.

Observe, that David speaks first to God and then to men. Surely we should all speak the more boldly to men if we had more constant converse with God. He who dares to face his Maker will not tremble before the sons of men.

The name by which the Lord is here addressed, “God of my righteousness,” deserves notice, since it is not used in any other part of Scripture. It means, Thou art the author, the witness, the maintainer, the judge, and the rewarder of my righteousness; to thee I appeal from the calumnies and harsh judgments of men. Herein is wisdom, let us imitate it and always take our suit, not to the petty courts of human opinion, but into the superior court, the King’s Bench of heaven.

You people, how long will my honor be dragged into disgrace? How long will you love empty things and go looking for lies? Selah Be sure of this: the LORD has set apart the one who is faithful to him as his own. The LORD will hear me when I call to him. Tremble, and do not sin. Lying on your bed, reason it out in your own heart, and be still. Selah Bring sacrifices as they should be brought, and rely on the LORD.

— Psalm 4:2–5

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

... And therefore leaving these, who are many, multiplied, that is, by the desire of things temporal, and who say, “Who showeth us good things?” which are to be sought not with the eyes without, but with simplicity of heart within, the faithful man rejoices and says, “In peace, together, I will sleep, and take rest” (ver. 8). For such men justly hope for all manner of estrangement of mind from things mortal, and forgetfulness of this world’s miseries; which is beautifully and prophetically signified under the name of sleep and rest, where the most perfect peace cannot be interrupted by any tumult. But this is not had now in this life, but is to be hoped for after this life. This even the words themselves, which are in the future tense, show us. For it is not said, either, I have slept, and taken rest; or, I do sleep, and take rest; but, “I will sleep, and take rest.” Then shall “this corruptible put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality; then shall death be swallowed up in victory.” Hence it is said, “But if we hope for that we see not, we wait in patience.”

Many are saying, “Who will let us see good times?” LORD, turn your shining face toward us. The joy you have put in my heart is greater than theirs at harvest, when grain and new wine overflow. I will lie down in peace and fall asleep at once, because it is you, LORD, and you alone, who let me live in safety.

— Psalm 4:6–8
fields.summary: David calls on God to answer him and tells others to trust God; God has given him more joy than a rich harvest, and he sleeps in peace. With Augustine and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 5
fields.body_html:
A prayer at daybreak

LORD, hear what I say; take note of my sighs. Listen to me crying for help, my King and my God, because it is to you that I pray. LORD, at daybreak you hear my voice. At daybreak I set everything out before you and keep watch.

— Psalm 5:1–3

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

Observe, this is not so much a prayer as a resolution, “‘ My voice shalt thou hear,’ I will not be dumb, I will not be silent, I will not withhold my speech, I will cry to thee, for the fire that dwells within compels me to pray.” We can sooner die than live without prayer. None of God’s children are possessed with a dumb devil.

“In the morning.” This is the fittest time for intercourse with God. An hour in the morning is worth two in the evening. While the dew is on the grass, let grace drop upon the soul. Let us give to God the mornings of our days and the morning of our lives. Prayer should be the key of the day and the lock of the night. Devotion should be both the morning star and the evening star.

If we merely read our English version, and want an explanation of these two sentences, we find it in the figure of an archer, “I will direct my prayer unto thee,” I will put my prayer upon the bow, I will direct it towards heaven, and then when I have shot up my arrow, I will look up to see where it has gone. But the Hebrew has a still fuller meaning than this —“I will direct my prayer.” It is the word that is used for the laying in order of the wood and the pieces of the victim upon the altar, and it is used also for the putting of the shewbread upon the table. It means just this: “I will arrange my prayer before thee;” I will lay it out upon the altar in the morning, just as the priest lays out the morning sacrifice. I will arrange my prayer; or, as old Master Trapp has it, “I will marshal up my prayers,” I will put them in order, call up all my powers, and bid them stand in their proper places, that I may pray with all my might, and pray acceptably.

For you are not a God who takes pleasure in wickedness; evil cannot be your guest. Those who boast cannot stand in your sight; you hate all who practice evil. You bring liars to ruin. The LORD loathes those who shed blood and deceive. But I, because your loyal love is so great, will come into your house; in awe of you I will bow down toward your holy temple.

— Psalm 5:4–7

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

... Farther, as our carnal minds either wickedly undervalue the grace of God, or put the low estimate upon it which is commonly put by the world, let us learn to extol its wonderful greatness, which is sufficient to enable us to overcome all fears. The primary object of David was to encourage himself in the assured hope of preservation from the mercy of God; but at the same time he shows, that upon obtaining deliverance, he will be grateful to God for it, and keep it in remembrance. And as hypocrites, in giving thanks to God, do nothing else but profane his name, inasmuch as they themselves are unholy and polluted, he therefore resolves to come in the fear of God, in order to worship him with a sincere and upright heard. Again, we may hence draw the general truth, that it is only through the goodness of God that we have access to him; and that no man prays aright but he who, having experienced his grace, believes and is fully persuaded that he will be merciful to him. The fear of God is at the same time added, in order to distinguish genuine and godly trust from the vain confidence of the flesh.

LORD, guide me in your righteousness, because my enemies are watching; level your road in front of me. Not one thing they say is reliable; deep inside them is only ruin. Their throats are graves left open, and their tongues are smooth with flattery. Hold them to account, God! Let them be tripped up by their own schemes. Thrust them away for all their many crimes, since it is against you that they have rebelled. But let everyone who makes you their refuge be glad and sing for joy forever. Keep them under your cover, and those who love your name will find their joy in you. For you bless the righteous, LORD; your favor surrounds them like a great shield.

— Psalm 5:8–12
fields.summary: David prays in the morning for God to hear him and lead him in righteousness, for God hates evil, and he asks God to protect those who take refuge in God. With John Calvin and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 6
fields.body_html:
A prayer from a bed of tears

LORD, when you correct me, do not do it in anger; when you discipline me, do not do it in your fury. Show me grace, LORD, for I am wasting away; heal me, LORD, for my very bones are shaking. My soul is shaken to its depths. But you, LORD, how long? Turn back to me, LORD, and set my life free; save me because your love is loyal.

— Psalm 6:1–4

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

Return, O Lord. In the preceding verses the Psalmist bewailed the absence of God, and now he earnestly requests the tokens of his presence, for our happiness consists in this, that we are the objects of the Divine regard, but we think he is alienated from us, if he does not give us some substantial evidence of his care for us. That David was at this time in the utmost peril, we gather from these words, in which he prays both for the deliverance of his soul, as it were, from the jaws of death, and for his restoration to a state of safety. Yet no mention is made of any bodily disease, and, therefore, I give no judgment with respect to the kind of his affliction. David, again, confirms what he had touched upon in the second verse concerning the mercy of God, namely, that this is the only quarter from which he hopes for deliverance: Save me for thy mercy’s sake Men will never find a remedy for their miseries until, forgetting their own merits, by trusting to which they only deceive themselves, they have learned to betake themselves to the free mercy of God.

For in death no one calls you to mind. Who gives you thanks down in Sheol? I am exhausted from groaning. Night after night my bed swims with my tears, and my couch dissolves in them. Grief has dimmed my eyes; they have aged because of all who oppose me. Get away from me, all who practice evil, for the LORD has heard me weeping. The LORD has heard me beg for his grace; the LORD welcomes my prayer. All my enemies will be put to shame and filled with terror; they will turn back, suddenly disgraced.

— Psalm 6:5–10

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

III. He either prays for the conversion or predicts the destruction of his enemies and persecutors, v. 10. 1. It may very well be taken as a prayer for their conversion: “Let them all be ashamed of the opposition they have given me and the censures they have passed upon me. Let them be (as all true penitents are) vexed at themselves for their own folly; let them return to a better temper and disposition of mind, and let them be ashamed of what they have done against me and take shame to themselves.” 2. If they be not converted, it is a prediction of their confusion and ruin. They shall be ashamed and sorely vexed (so it maybe read), and that justly. They rejoiced that David was vexed (v. 2, 3), and therefore, as usually happens, the evil returns upon themselves; they also shall be sorely vexed. Those that will not give glory to God shall have their faces filled with everlasting shame.

In singing this, and praying over it, we must give glory to God, as a God ready to hear prayer, must own his goodness to us in hearing our prayers, and must encourage ourselves to wait upon him and to trust in him in the greatest straits and difficulties.
fields.summary: In distress and illness David begs God not to correct him in anger; worn out with weeping, he is sure that God has heard his cry. With John Calvin and Matthew Henry.

fields.title: Psalm 7
fields.body_html:
A plea to the righteous judge

LORD my God, I have made you my refuge. Save me from all who are hunting me down, and rescue me,

— Psalm 7:1

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

“O Lord my God, in Thee have I hoped: save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me” (ver. 1). As one to whom, already perfected, all the war and enmity of vice being overcome, there remaineth no enemy but the envious devil, he says, “Save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me (ver. 2): lest at any time he tear my soul as a lion.” The Apostle says, “Your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.” Therefore when the Psalmist said in the plural number, “Save me from all them that persecute me:” he afterwards introduced the singular, saying, “lest at any time he tear my soul as a lion.” For he does not say, lest at any time they tear: he knew what enemy and violent adversary of the perfect soul remained. “Whilst there be none to redeem, nor to save:” that is, lest he tear me, whilst Thou redeemest not, nor savest. For, if God redeem not, nor save, he tears.

3. And that it might be clear that the already perfect soul, which is to be on her guard against the most insidious snares of the devil only, says this, see what follows....

or he will tear me apart like a lion, dragging me off with no one to rescue me. LORD my God, if I have done what they say, if my hands are guilty of wrong, if I have paid back a friend with harm, or robbed my enemy for no reason, then let my enemy chase me down and catch me; let him trample my life into the ground and leave my honor lying in the dust. Selah Rise up, LORD, in your anger! Stand up against the rage of my enemies. Wake up and act for me; you have ordered justice to be done. Let the peoples gather around you, and take your seat again above them on high. The LORD judges the peoples. Give me justice, LORD, because I am in the right and have done no wrong. Bring the evil of the wicked to an end, and make the righteous secure, for you are the righteous God who tests minds and hearts. My shield is God, who rescues those whose hearts are right. God is a righteous judge, a God who is angry at evil every day. If anyone will not turn back, God will sharpen his sword; he has strung his bow and taken aim. He has made ready deadly weapons for that person, and he turns his arrows into fire. See how the wicked person is pregnant with evil: having conceived trouble, he gives birth to lies. He dug a pit and scooped it out deep, and fell into the very hole he made. The trouble he caused comes back on his own head; his violence falls on his own skull.

— Psalm 7:2–16

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

II. He is no less confident of the destruction of all his persecutors, even as many of them as would not repent, to give glory to God. He reads their doom here, for their good, if possible, that they might cease from their enmity, or, however, for his own comfort, that he might not be afraid of them nor aggrieved at their prosperity and success for a time. He goes into the sanctuary of God, and there understands,

1. That they are children of wrath. They are not to be envied, for God is angry with them, is angry with the wicked every day. They are every day doing that which is provoking to him, and he resents it, and treasures it up against the day of wrath. As his mercies are new every morning towards his people, so his anger is new every morning against the wicked, upon the fresh occasions given for it by their renewed transgressions. God is angry with the wicked even in the merriest and most prosperous of their days, even in the days of their devotion; for, if they be suffered to prosper, it is in wrath; if they pray, their very prayers are an abomination. The wrath of God abides upon them (John iii. 36) and continual additions are made to it.

I will thank the LORD because he does what is right, and I will sing praises to the name of the LORD Most High.

— Psalm 7:17

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

We conclude with the joyful contrast. In this all these Psalms are agreed; they all exhibit the blessedness of the righteous, and make its colours the more glowing by contrast with the miseries of the wicked. The bright jewel sparkles in a black foil. Praise is the occupation of the godly, their eternal work, and their present pleasure. Singing is the fitting embodiment for praise, and therefore do the saints make melody before the Lord Most High. The slandered one is now a singer: his harp was unstrung for a very little season, and now we leave him sweeping its harmonious chords, and flying on their music to the third heaven of adoring praise.
fields.summary: David takes refuge in God against those who pursue him and asks God, the righteous judge, to vindicate him. With Augustine, Matthew Henry and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 8
fields.body_html:
Your name across the whole earth

LORD, our Lord, how glorious is your name across the whole earth! Your splendor reaches higher than the heavens. Out of the mouths of children and babies at the breast you have built a stronghold against your foes, to silence the enemy and the one bent on revenge.

— Psalm 8:1–2

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

... Whence is it that nourishment is ready for them as soon as they are born, but because God wonderfully changes blood into milk? Whence, also, have they the skill to suck, but because the same God has, by a mysterious instinct, fitted their tongues for doing this? David, therefore, has the best reason for declaring, that although the tongues of all, who have arrived at the age of manhood, should become silent, the speechless mouth of infants is sufficiently able to celebrate the praise of God. And when he not only introduces babes as witnesses and preachers of God’s glory, but also attributes mature strength to their mouth, the expression is very emphatic. It means the same thing as if he had said, These are invincible champions of God who, when it comes to the conflict, can easily scatter and discomfit the whole host of the wicked despisers of God, and those who have abandoned themselves to impiety. We should observe against whom he imposes upon infants the office of defending the glory of God, namely, against the hardened despisers of God, who dare to rise up against heaven to make war upon God, as the poets have said, in olden time, of the giants.

When I look up at your heavens, which your fingers made, at the moon and stars you have fixed in their places, what are human beings, that you keep them in mind, mere mortals, that you look after them? You made them only a little less than God and set a crown of glory and honor on them. You made them rulers over all that your hands have made; you put everything under their feet: sheep and cattle, all of them, and the wild animals too, the birds of the air and the fish of the sea, and everything that travels the paths of the seas.

— Psalm 8:3–8

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

These verses may set forth man’s position among the creatures before he fell; but as they are, by the apostle Paul, appropriated to man as represented by the Lord Jesus, it is best to give most weight to that meaning. In order of dignity, man stood next to the angels, and a little lower than they; in the Lord Jesus this was accomplished, for he was made a little lower than the angels by the suffering of death. Man in Eden had the full command of all creatures, and they came before him to receive their names as an act of homage to him as the vicegerent of God to them. Jesus in his glory, is now Lord, not only of all living, but of all created things, and, with the exception of him who put all things under him, Jesus is Lord of all, and his elect, in him, are raised to a dominion wider than that of the first Adam, as shall be more clearly seen at his coming. Well might the Psalmist wonder at the singular exaltation of man in the scale of being, when he marked his utter nothingness in comparison with the starry universe.

LORD, our Lord, how glorious is your name across the whole earth!

— Psalm 8:9
fields.summary: God’s name is glorious in all the earth; when David looks at the heavens he wonders that God cares for human beings and has crowned them with glory over all creation. With John Calvin and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 9
fields.body_html:
Thanks to the judge of the world

I will thank the LORD with my whole heart; I will tell of all the wonderful things you have done. I will be glad and celebrate because of you; I will sing praises to your name, Most High. When my enemies turn and retreat, they stumble and are destroyed in your presence. For you have taken up my case and given me justice; you sat on your throne as a judge who does what is right.

— Psalm 9:1–4

A. R. Fausset · Commentary, Critical and Explanatory

Ps 9:1-20. Upon Muthlabben, or, after the manner according to “death to the Son,” by which some song was known, to whose air or melody the musician is directed to perform this Psalm. This mode of denoting a song by some prominent word or words is still common (compare Ps 22:1). The Psalmist praises God for deliverance from his enemies and celebrates the divine government, for providing security to God’s people and punishment to the wicked. Thus encouraging himself, he prays for new occasions to recount God’s mercies, and confident of His continued judgment on the wicked and vindication of the oppressed, he implores a prompt and efficient manifestation of the divine sovereignty.

You have rebuked the nations and brought the wicked to ruin; you have wiped their name away for all time.

— Psalm 9:5

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

God rebukes before he destroys, but when he once comes to blows with the wicked he ceases not until he has dashed them in pieces so small that their very name is forgotten, and like a noisome snuff their remembrance is put out for ever and ever. How often the word “thou” occurs in this and the former verse, to show us that the grateful strain mounts up directly to the Lord as doth the smoke from the altar when the air is still. My soul send up all the music of all thy powers to him who has been and is thy sure deliverance.

The enemy is finished, left in ruins forever; you have torn up their cities by the roots, and no one remembers them now.

— Psalm 9:6

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

... These cities He destroys, when on the prince being shut out thence, of whom it was said, “The prince of this world” has been “cast out,” these kingdoms are wasted by the word of truth, evil counsels are laid to sleep, vile affections tamed, the ministries of the members and senses taken captive, and transferred to the service of righteousness and good works: that as the Apostle says, “Sin should no more reign in” our “mortal body,” and so forth. Then is the soul at peace, and the man is disposed to receive rest and blessedness. “Their memorial has perished with uproar:” with the uproar, that is, of the ungodly. But it is said, “with uproar,” either because when ungodliness is overturned, there is uproar made: for none passeth to the highest place, where there is the deepest silence, but he who with much uproar shall first have warred with his own vices: or “with uproar,” is said, that the memory of the ungodly should perish in the perishing even of the very uproar, in which ungodliness riots.

But the LORD remains on his throne forever; it is a throne he has set up to judge from. He will judge the world rightly and govern the peoples with fairness. The LORD is a fortress on the heights for those who are crushed, a safe height in times of trouble. Those who know your name will rely on you, because you do not desert anyone who comes looking for you, LORD. Make music to the LORD, whose throne is in Zion! Announce his deeds among the peoples. For the God who calls murderers to account remembers the victims; he has not overlooked the cry of those who suffer. Show me grace, LORD! See how my enemies make me suffer, you who lift me up from the gates of death, so that in the gates of the city of Zion I may tell all the reasons you are praised, and be glad that you saved me.

— Psalm 9:7–14

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

That I may recount. David’s meaning simply is, that he will celebrate the praises of God in all assemblies, and, wherever there is the greatest concourse of people, (for at that time it was the custom to hold assemblies at the gates of cities;) but, at the same time, there seems to be an allusion to the gates of death, of which he has just spoken, as if he had said, After I am delivered from the grave, I will do my endeavor to bear testimony, in the most public manner, to the goodness of God, manifested in my deliverance. As, however, it is not sufficient to utter the praises of God with our tongues, if they do not proceed from the heart, the Psalmist, in the last clause of the verse, expresses the inward joy with which he would engage in this exercise, And that I may rejoice in thy salvation; as if he had said, I desire to live in this world for no other purpose than to rejoice in having been preserved by the grace of God. Under the name of daughter, as is well known, the Jews meant a people or city, but he here names the city from its principal part, namely, Sion.

The nations have sunk down into the very pit they dug; the net they hid has snared their own feet. The LORD has made himself known by doing justice: he snares the wicked in the work of their own hands. Higgaion. Selah The wicked will go back down to Sheol, every nation that forgets God.

— Psalm 9:15–17

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

In the other world (v. 17): The wicked shall be turned into hell, as captives into the prison-house, even all the nations that forget God. Note, (1.) Forgetfulness of God is the cause of all the wickedness of the wicked. (2.) There are nations of those that forget God, multitudes that live without God in the world, many great and many mighty nations, that never regard him nor desire the knowledge of his ways. (3.) Hell will, at last, be the portion of such, a state of everlasting misery and torment—Sheol, a pit of destruction, in which they and all their comforts will be for ever lost and buried. Though there be nations of them, yet they shall be turned into hell, like sheep into the slaughter-house (Ps. xlix. 14), and their being so numerous will not be any security or ease to them, nor any loss to God or the least impeachment of his goodness.

For the needy will not always be forgotten, nor will the hope of the poor be lost forever. Rise up, LORD! Do not let mere humans win. Bring the nations to judgment before you. Fill them with fear, LORD, and let the nations find out they are nothing but human. Selah

— Psalm 9:18–20
fields.summary: David thanks God for judging the nations with justice and for being a stronghold for the oppressed, who are not forgotten. With Augustine, John Calvin, Matthew Henry and 2 more.

fields.title: Psalm 10
fields.body_html:
Why do you keep so far away?

LORD, why do you keep so far away? Why do you hide yourself when trouble comes? In their arrogance the wicked hunt down the poor. Let them be trapped in the very schemes they have dreamed up! The wicked brag about what they crave; the greedy bless themselves while they treat the LORD with contempt. With their noses in the air, the wicked never seek God. All their scheming says, “There is no God.” Their ways always seem to succeed; your judgments are high above them, out of their sight; they sneer at all their enemies.

— Psalm 10:1–5

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

“God is not in his sight, his ways are polluted in all time” (ver. 5). He that knows what in the soul gives joy and gladness, knows how great an ill it is to be abandoned by the light of truth: since a great ill do men reckon the blindness of their bodily eyes, whereby this light is withdrawn. How great then the punishment he endures, who through the prosperous issue of his sins is brought to that pass, that God is not in his sight, and that his ways are polluted in all time, that is, his thoughts and counsels are unclean! “Thy judgments are taken away from his face.” For the mind conscious of evil, whilst it seems to itself to suffer no punishment, believes that God doth not judge, and so are God’s judgments taken away from its face; while this very thing is great condemnation. “And he shall have dominion over all his enemies.” For so is it delivered, that he will overcome all kings, and alone obtain the kingdom; since too according to the Apostle, who preaches concerning him, “He shall sit in the temple of God, exalting himself above all that is worshipped and that is called God.”

“Nothing can shake me,” they tell themselves; “I will never come to harm, now or ever.” Their mouths are full of curses, lies and threats; they keep mischief and wrongdoing ready under the tongue.

— Psalm 10:6–7

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

Let us now hear the witnesses in court. Let the wretch speak for himself, for out of his own mouth he will be condemned. “His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud.” There is not only a little evil there, but his mouth is full of it. A three-headed serpent hath stowed away its coils and venom within the den of his black mouth. There is cursing which he spits against both God and men, deceit with which he entraps the unwary, and fraud by which, even in his common dealings, he robs his neighbours. Beware of such a man: have no sort of dealing with him: none but the silliest of geese would go to the fox’s sermon, and none but the most foolish will put themselves into the society of knaves. But we must proceed. Let us look under this man’s tongue as well as in his mouth; “under his tongue is mischief and vanity.” Deep in his throat are the unborn words which shall come forth as mischief and iniquity.

They lie in wait near the villages and murder the innocent from hiding; their eyes are on the lookout for the helpless. They crouch in hiding like a lion in its thicket, waiting to grab the poor; they grab them and haul them away in their nets. The weak are crushed and bowed down; the helpless fall into their strong grip. They tell themselves, “God has forgotten; he has turned his face away and will never see.” Rise up, LORD! God, raise your hand! Do not forget those who suffer. Why do the wicked treat God with contempt and tell themselves, “You will not call us to account”? But you do see! You take note of trouble and grief and take the matter into your own hands. The helpless entrust themselves to you; you have always helped the orphan. Break the power of the wicked and the evildoer; hunt down their wickedness until there is none left to find. The LORD reigns as King for all time; the nations are gone from his land.

— Psalm 10:8–16

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

... Hitherto they shall come, but no further; here shall the proud waves of their malice be stayed; an effectual course shall be taken that the man of the earth may no more oppress. See how light the psalmist now makes of the power of that proud persecutor whom he had been describing in this psalm, and how slightly he speaks of him now that he had been considering God’s sovereignty. First, He is but a man of the earth, a man out of the earth (so the word is), sprung out of the earth, and therefore mean, and weak, and hastening to the earth again. Why then should we be afraid of the fury of the oppressor when he is but man that shall die, a son of man that shall be as grass? Isa. li. 12. He that protects us is the Lord of heaven; he that persecutes us is but a man of the earth. Secondly, God has him in a chain, and can easily restrain the remainder of his wrath, so that he cannot do what he would. When God speaks the word Satan shall by his instruments no more deceive (Rev. xx. 3), no more oppress.

LORD, you have heard what the humble long for; you steady their hearts and bend down to listen, to give justice to the orphan and the oppressed, so that mere mortals made of earth will strike terror no more.

— Psalm 10:17–18
fields.summary: The psalmist asks why God seems far away while the wicked hunt down the poor, and calls on God to rise up, for God hears the afflicted and defends the fatherless. With Augustine, Matthew Henry and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 11
fields.body_html:
Refuge when the foundations give way

For the music director. Of David. I have taken refuge in the LORD. How can you say to me, “Escape to the hills like a bird! Look, the wicked have their bows bent and their arrows set on the string, ready to shoot under cover of darkness at those whose hearts are right.

— Psalm 11:1–2

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

... Whom certain heretics being ignorant of, and not able to discern Him, endeavour to turn away the minds of the simple to this corporeal and visible sun, which is the common light of the flesh of men and flies, and some they do pervert, who as long as they cannot behold with the mind the inner light of truth, will not be content with the simple Catholic faith; which is the only safety to babes, and by which milk alone they can arrive in assured strength at the firm support of more solid food. Whichever then of these two opinions be the true, the moon in allegory is fitly understood as the Church. Or if in such difficulties as these, troublesome rather than edifying, there be either no satisfaction or no leisure to exercise the mind, or if the mind itself be not capable of it, it is sufficient to regard the moon with ordinary eyes, and not to seek out obscure causes, but with all men to perceive her increasings and fulnesses and wanings; and if she wanes to the end that she may be renewed, even to this rude multitude she sets forth the image of the Church, in which the resurrection of the dead is believed.

“If the very pillars that hold things up are pulled down, what can the righteous accomplish?” The LORD is in his holy temple; the throne of the LORD is in heaven. His eyes watch; his gaze examines every human being. The LORD tests the righteous, but he hates with all his being the wicked and those who love violence. On the wicked he will rain down snares; fire, burning sulfur and a scorching wind will be the cup they are given. For the LORD is righteous and loves what is right; those who are upright will look on his face.

— Psalm 11:3–7

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

David here declares the great source of his unflinching courage. He borrows his light from heaven — from the great central orb of deity. The God of the believer is never far from him; he is not merely the God of the mountain fastnesses, but of the dangerous valleys and battle plains.

“Jehovah is in his holy temple.” The heavens are above our heads in all regions of the earth, and so is the Lord ever near to us in every state and condition. This is a very strong reason why we should not adopt the vile suggestions of distrust. There is one who pleads his precious blood in our behalf in the temple above, and there is one upon the throne who is never deaf to the intercession of his Son. Why, then, should we fear? What plots can men devise which Jesus will not discover? Satan has doubtless desired to have us, that he may sift us as wheat, but Jesus is in the temple praying for us, and how can our faith fail? What attempts can the wicked make which Jehovah shall not behold? And since he is in his holy temple, delighting in the sacrifice of his Son, will he not defeat every device, and send us a sure deliverance?
fields.summary: When advised to flee like a bird, David declares that he takes refuge in God, who sees from heaven and loves justice. With Augustine and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 12
fields.body_html:
Pure words in a time of lies

Save us, LORD! The faithful are no more; no one you can trust is left among humankind. People tell each other lies; their lips are smooth with flattery, their hearts are divided.

— Psalm 12:1–2

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

When dissimulation and flattery have corrupted and debauched all conversation, then the times are very bad (v. 2), when men are generally so profligate that they make no conscience of a lie, are so spiteful as to design against their neighbours the worst of mischiefs, and yet so base as to cover the design with the most specious and plausible pretences and professions of friendship. Thus they speak vanity (that is, falsehood and a lie) every one to his neighbour, with flattering lips and a double heart. They will kiss and kill (as Joab did Abner and Amasa in David’s own time), will smile in your face and cut your throat. This is the devil’s image complete, a complication of malice and falsehood. The times are bad indeed when there is no such thing as sincerity to be met with, when an honest man knows not whom to believe nor whom to trust, nor dares put confidence in a friend, in a guide, Mic. vii. 5, 6; Jer. ix. 4, 5. Woe to those who help to make the times thus perilous.

May the LORD cut off every flattering lip and every tongue that boasts so loudly, those who say, “Our tongues will win the day; our lips are our own. Who can be master over us?” “The poor are being robbed and the needy are groaning, so now I will get up,” says the LORD. “I will bring them to the safety they long for.”

— Psalm 12:3–5

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

“Because of the wretchedness of the needy and the sighing of the poor, now I will arise, saith the Lord” (ver. 5). For so the Lord Himself in the Gospel pitied His people, because they had no ruler, when they could well obey. Whence too it is said in the Gospel, “The harvest is plenteous, but the labourers are few.” But this must be taken as spoken in the person of God the Father, who, because of the needy and the poor, that is, who in need and poverty were lacking spiritual good things, vouchsafed to send His own Son. From thence begins His sermon on the mount to Matthew, where He says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” “I will place in salvation.” He does not say what He would place: but, “in salvation,” must be understood as, in Christ; according to that, “For mine eyes have seen Thy salvation.” And hence He is understood to have placed in Him what appertains to the taking away the wretchedness of the needy, and the comforting the sighing of the poor. “I will deal confidently in Him:” according to that in the Gospel, “For He taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes.”

The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a clay furnace, purified seven times over. You, LORD, will watch over them; you will protect each of them from this generation forever. On every side the wicked prowl, while what is vile is prized among people.

— Psalm 12:6–8
fields.summary: When the faithful have vanished and everyone speaks lies, God promises to rise up for the poor, and God’s words are pure as refined silver. With Augustine and Matthew Henry.

fields.title: Psalm 13
fields.body_html:
How long, LORD?

How long, LORD? Will you go on forgetting me for good? How long will you turn your face away from me? How long must I keep turning plans over in my mind, with grief in my heart all day long? How long will my enemy stand over me in triumph?

— Psalm 13:1–2

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

“How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” (ver. 2). There is no need of counsel but in adversity. Therefore “How long shall I place counsel in my soul?” is as if it were said, How long shall I be in adversity? Or at least it is an answer, so that the meaning is this, So long, O Lord, wilt Thou forget me to the end, and so long turn away Thy face from me, until I shall place counsel in mine own soul: so that except a man place counsel in his own soul to work mercy perfectly, God will not direct him to the end, nor give him that full knowledge of Himself, which is “face to face.” “Sorrow in my heart through the day?” How long shall I have, is understood. And “through the day” signifies continuance, so that day is taken for time: from which as each one longs to be free, he has sorrow in his heart, making entreaty to rise to things eternal, and not endure man’s day.

3. “How long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?” either the devil, or carnal habit.

Turn and look, LORD my God, and answer me! Bring the light back to my eyes, or I will fall asleep in death, and my enemy will say, “I have beaten him,” and those against me will celebrate when I stumble.

— Psalm 13:3–4

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

Lest my enemy. David again repeats what he had a little before said concerning the pride of his enemies, namely, how it would be a thing ill becoming the character of God were he to abandon his servant to the mockery of the ungodly. David’s enemies lay, as it were, in ambush watching the hour of his ruin, that they might deride him when they saw him fall. And as it is the peculiar office of God to repress the audacity and insolence of the wicked, as often as they glory in their wickedness, David beseeches God to deprive them of the opportunity of indulging in such boasting. It is, however, to be observed, that he had in his conscience a sufficient testimony to his own integrity, and that he trusted also in the goodness of his cause, so that it would have been unbecoming and unreasonable had he been left without succor in danger, and had he been overwhelmed by his enemies. We can, therefore, with confidence pray for ourselves, in the manner in which David here does for himself, only when we fight under the standard of God, and are obedient to his orders, so that our enemies cannot obtain the victory over us without wickedly triumphing over God himself.

But I trust in your loyal love; my heart will be glad because you save. I will sing to the LORD, because he has been so generous to me.

— Psalm 13:5
fields.summary: David asks how long God will forget him, then trusts in God’s loyal love and sings of God’s goodness. With Augustine and John Calvin.

fields.title: Psalm 14
fields.body_html:
No one who does good

For the music director. Of David. Fools tell themselves, “There is no God.” They are rotten through and through; what they do is detestable. Not one of them does good. From heaven the LORD looks down on the human race to see whether anyone is wise, anyone who is looking for God.

— Psalm 14:1–2

Augustine · Expositions on the Psalms

“The Lord from heaven looked out upon the sons of men, to see if there be one understanding, or seeking after God” (ver. 2). It may be interpreted, upon the Jews; as he may have given them the more honourable name of the sons of men, by reason of their worship of the One God, in comparison with the Gentiles; of whom I suppose it was said above, “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God,” etc. Now the Lord looks out, that He may see, by His holy souls: which is the meaning of, “from heaven.” For by Himself nothing is hid from Him.

4. “All have gone out of the way, they have together become useless:” that is, the Jews have become as the Gentiles, who were spoken of above....

Everyone has left the road; all alike have gone bad. No one does good, not a single one.

— Psalm 14:3

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

(2.) The disgrace and debasement it puts upon the nature of man. Sinners are corrupt, quite degenerated from what man was in his innocent estate: They have become filthy (v. 3), putrid. All their faculties are so disordered that they have become odious to their Maker and utterly incapable of answering the ends of their creation. They are corrupt indeed; for, [1.] They do no good, but are the unprofitable burdens of the earth; they do God no service, bring him no honour, nor do themselves any real kindness. [2.] They do a great deal of hurt. They have done abominable works, for such all sinful works are. Sin is an abomination to God; it is that abominable thing which he hates (Jer. xliv. 4), and, sooner or later, it will be so to the sinner; it will be found to be hateful (Ps. xxxvi. 2), an abomination of desolation, that is, making desolate, Matt. xxiv. 15. This follows upon their saying, There is no God; for those that profess they know God, but in works deny him, are abominable, and to every good work reprobate, Tit. i. 16.

Have they learned nothing, all these evildoers? They devour my people as if they were eating bread, and they never call on the LORD. There they will be gripped by terror, because God is with the people who are righteous. You evildoers would make the hopes of the poor come to nothing, but the LORD is their shelter. If only Zion would send Israel its rescue! When the LORD turns back the fortunes of his people, let Jacob shout for joy and Israel be glad.

— Psalm 14:4–7

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

... I will not deny that the Psalmist, by the spirit of prophecy, may have predicted what had not yet actually taken place; but I think it highly probable, that this psalm was not composed until the ark of the covenant had been placed on mount Sion. David, as we know, employed his leisure hours in committing to writing, for the benefit of posterity, events which had happened long before. Besides, by expressing his desire for the deliverance of Israel, we are taught that he was chiefly anxious about the welfare of the whole body of the Church, and that his thoughts were more occupied about this than about himself individually. This is worthy of being the more carefully marked when we consider, that, while our attention is engrossed with our own particular sorrows, we are in danger of almost entirely neglecting the welfare of our brethren. And yet the particular afflictions with which God visits each of us are intended to admonish us to direct our attention and care to the whole body of the Church, and to think of its necessities, just as we see David here including Israel with himself.
fields.summary: Fools say there is no God, and no one does good, yet God is with the righteous and will restore the fortunes of God’s people. With Augustine, John Calvin and Matthew Henry.

fields.title: Psalm 15
fields.body_html:
Who may stay in God’s tent?

A psalm of David. LORD, who may stay as a guest in your tent? Who may make a home on your holy mountain? Whoever walks without blame, practices what is right, and speaks truth that comes from the heart,

— Psalm 15:1–2

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

III. The psalm concludes with a ratification of this character of the citizen of Zion. He is like Zion-hill itself, which cannot be moved, but abides for ever, Ps. cxxv. 1. Every true living member of the church, like the church itself, is built upon a rock, which the gates of hell cannot prevail against: He that doeth these things shall never be moved; shall not be moved for ever, so the word is. The grace of God shall always be sufficient for him, to preserve him safe and blameless to the heavenly kingdom. Temptations shall not overcome him, troubles shall not overwhelm him, nothing shall rob him of his present peace nor his future bliss.

In singing this psalm we must teach and admonish ourselves, and one another, to answer the characters here given of the citizen of Zion, that we may never be moved from God’s tabernacle on earth, and may arrive, at last, at that holy hill where we shall be for ever out of the reach of temptation and danger.

who does not go around spreading slander, does no harm to a neighbor, and does not heap insults on those close by,

— Psalm 15:3

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

... He employs these terms to show more clearly the odiousness of what he condemns, and that the saints may have the greater abhorrence of all wrong dealing, since every man who hurts his neighbor violates the fundamental law of human society. With respect to the meaning of the last clause, interpreters are not agreed. Some take the phrase, to raise up a calumnious report, for to invent, because malicious persons raise up calumnies from nothing; and thus it would be a repetition of the statement contained in the first clause of the verse, namely, that good men should not allow themselves to indulge in detraction. But I think there is also here rebuked the vice of undue credulity, which, when any evil reports are spread against our neighbors, leads us either eagerly to listen to them, or at least to receive them without sufficient reason; whereas we ought rather to use all means to suppress and trample them under foot. When any one is the bearer of invented falsehoods, those who reject them leave them, as it were, to fall to the ground; while, on the contrary, those who propagate and publish them from one person to another are, by an expressive form of speech, said to raise them up.

who looks with contempt on one who is rejected but shows honor to all who fear the LORD, and who stands by a sworn promise at personal cost, never going back on it. who does not lend money to make a profit from interest, and will not take a bribe to harm the innocent. Anyone who lives like this will stand firm forever.

— Psalm 15:4–5
fields.summary: David asks who may dwell on God’s holy mountain: the one who walks without blame, speaks truth and keeps his word. With John Calvin and Matthew Henry.

fields.title: Psalm 16
fields.body_html:
My share is the LORD

A miktam of David. Guard me, God, for I have made you my refuge. My soul, you have told the LORD, “You are my Lord; my good is found in you alone.” The holy people who live in the land are the truly great; they are my whole delight. Those who court another god will have sorrow upon sorrow. I will not pour out their offerings of blood, or even speak the names of their gods. The LORD is the share I have been given and the cup I drink; it is you who hold my lot secure. The measuring lines have marked out a lovely place for me; truly, the land I inherit delights me. I bless the LORD, my adviser; even at night my deepest self keeps teaching me.

— Psalm 16:1–7

A. R. Fausset · Commentary, Critical and Explanatory

... In referring the whole Psalm to Christ, it is, however, by no means denied that much of its language is expressive of the feelings of His people, so far as in their humble measure they have the feelings of trust in God expressed by Him, their head and representative. Such use of His language, as recorded in His last prayer (Joh 17:1-26), and even that which He used in Gethsemane, under similar modifications, is equally proper. The propriety of this reference of the Psalm to Christ will appear in the scope and interpretation. In view of the sufferings before Him, the Saviour, with that instinctive dread of death manifested in Gethsemane, calls on God to “preserve” Him; He avows His delight in holiness and abhorrence of the wicked and their wickedness; and for “the joy that was set before Him, despising the shame” [Heb 12:2], encourages Himself; contemplating the glories of the heritage appointed Him. Thus even death and the grave lose their terrors in the assurance of the victory to be attained and “the glory that should follow” [1Pe 1:11].

I have placed the LORD in front of me at all times; since he is there at my right hand, I will never stumble. That is why my heart is glad and my spirit celebrates; my body too will live in safety. For you will not give me up to Sheol, nor allow your loyal one to see the pit. You teach me the road that leads to life; in your presence there is joy in full, and at your right hand delights that never end.

— Psalm 16:8–11

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

... We have little to hope for from this life, but we shall rest in hope of a better life; we may put off the body in that hope. Death destroys the hope of man (Job xiv. 19), but not the hope of a good Christian, Prov. xiv. 32. He has hope in his death, living hopes in dying moments, hopes that the body shall not be left for ever in the grave, but, though it see corruption for a time, it shall, at the end of the time, be raised to immortality; Christ’s resurrection is an earnest of ours if we be his. 4. That those who live piously with God in their eye may die comfortably with heaven in their eye. In this world sorrow is our lot, but in heaven there is joy. All our joys here are empty and defective, but in heaven there is a fulness of joy. Our pleasures here are transient and momentary, and such is the nature of them that it is not fit they should last long; but those at God’s right hand are pleasures for evermore; for they are the pleasures of immortal souls in the immediate vision and fruition of an eternal God.
fields.summary: David has made God his refuge and his portion; he will not be abandoned to the grave but shown the path of life and fullness of joy. With Matthew Henry and A. R. Fausset.

fields.title: Psalm 17
fields.body_html:
Hide me in the shadow of your wings

A prayer of David. Hear a just cause, LORD; listen closely to my cry. Turn your ear to my prayer, which comes from lips that do not lie. Let my verdict come from you; let your eyes see what is fair. You have tested my heart and come to me in the night; you have put me through the fire and found nothing wrong. I have made up my mind not to sin with my mouth.

— Psalm 17:1–3

Matthew Henry · Commentary on the Whole Bible

What the evidence is by which he hopes to make good his appeal; it is the trial God had made of him (v. 3): Thou hast proved my heart. God’s sentence is therefore right, because he always proceeds upon his knowledge, which is more certain and infallible than that which men attain to by the closest views and the strictest investigations.

(1.) He knew God had tried him, [1.] By his own conscience, which is God’s deputy in the soul. The spirit of a man is the candle of the Lord, with this God had searched him, and visited him in the night, when he communed with his own heart upon his bed. He had submitted to the search, and had seriously reviewed the actions of his life, to discover what was amiss, but could find nothing of that which his enemies charged him with. [2.] By providence. God had tried him by the fair opportunity he had, once and again, to kill Saul; he had tried him by the malice of Saul, the treachery of his friends, and the many provocations that were given him; so that, if he had been the man he was represented to be, it would have appeared; but, upon all these trials, there was nothing found against him, no proof at all of the things whereof they accused him.

Whatever others may do, I have kept to the word that comes from your lips and stayed off the roads of the violent. My steps have held to your tracks; my feet have never slid. I call to you, for you answer me, God; bend your ear toward me and listen to what I say. Show your loyal love in a wonderful way, you who by your right hand save those who come to you for shelter from their attackers. Guard me as one guards the pupil of the eye; shelter me under the shade of your wings, from the wicked who attack me, from deadly enemies who close in around me.

— Psalm 17:4–9

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

“From the wicked that oppress me, from my deadly enemies, who compass me about.” The foes from whom David sought to be rescued were wicked men. It is hopeful for us when our enemies are God’s enemies. They were deadly enemies, whom nothing but his death would satisfy. The foes of a believer’s soul are mortal foes most emphatically, for they who war against our faith aim at the very life of our life. Deadly sins are deadly enemies, and what sin is there which hath not death in its bowels? These foes oppressed David, they laid his spirit waste, as invading armies ravage a country, or as wild beasts desolate a land. He likens himself to a besieged city, and complains that his foes compass him about. It may well quicken our business upward, when all around us, every road, is blockaded by deadly foes. This is our daily position, for all around us dangers and sins are lurking. O God, do thou protect us from them all.

They have shut up their hearts, hardened with fat; their mouths speak proud words. Now they track our steps and surround us; their eyes are fixed on throwing us to the ground,

— Psalm 17:10–11

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

... To fix their eyes, therefore, is nothing else than to apply all their ingenuity, and put forth all their efforts. What follows, to cast down to the ground, is the same thing as to overthrow. The ungodly, as if they must necessarily fall, should the world continue to stand, would wish all mankind thrown down or destroyed, and, therefore, they exert themselves to the utmost to bring down and ruin all men. This is explained more fully by the figurative illustration introduced in the following verse, where they are said to be like lions and lions’ whelps But we ought always to keep this truth in remembrance, that the more proudly wicked men exercise their cruelty against us, the hand of God is so much the nearer to us to oppose itself to their savage fury; for to him alone belongs the praise of subduing and restraining these wild beasts who delight in shedding blood. David speaks of dens, or secret lurking places, because his enemies were deeply skilled in artful stratagem, and had various methods of doing mischief, while they had also at hand the power and means of executing them, so that it was difficult to resist them.

like a lion eager to tear its prey, like a young lion crouching in its lair. Rise up, LORD! Meet them face to face and bring them to their knees. Rescue me from the wicked with your sword, from such people, LORD, by your hand, from people of this world whose share is in this life alone. You fill their stomachs with what you have stored up; their children have plenty, and they leave what is left to their little ones. But I, in the right, will look on your face; when I wake up, the sight of you will be all I want.

— Psalm 17:12–15
fields.summary: David appeals to God to hear his just cause and to hide him in the shadow of God’s wings from the wicked. With John Calvin, Matthew Henry and C. H. Spurgeon.

fields.title: Psalm 18
fields.body_html:
David’s song of rescue and victory

He said: “I love you, LORD, my strength.

— Psalm 18:1

C. H. Spurgeon · The Treasury of David

“I will love thee, O Lord.” With strong, hearty affection will I cling to thee; as a child to its parent, or a spouse to her husband. The word is intensely forcible, the love is of the deepest kind. “I will love heartily, with my inmost bowels.” Here is a fixed resolution to abide in the nearest and most intimate union with the Most High. Our triune God deserves the warmest love of all our hearts. Father, Son and Spirit have each a claim upon our love. The solemn purpose never to cease loving naturally springs from present fervour of affection, It is wrong to make rash resolutions, but this when made in the strength of God is most wise and fitting. “My strength.” Our God is the strength of our life, our graces, our works, our hopes, our conflicts, our victories. This verse is not found in 1 Sam. xxii., and is a most precious addition, placed above all and after all to form the pinnacle of the temple, the apex of the pyramid. Love is still the crowning grace.

“The LORD is my cliff, my stronghold, the one who sets me free; my God is my rock, and I shelter in him. He is my shield, my strong salvation, my tower on the heights. I call on the LORD, who is worthy of praise, and from my enemies I am rescued. Death’s ropes were wrapped around me; floods of ruin overwhelmed me with terror. The ropes of Sheol coiled around me; death’s traps lay right in front of me. When I was hard pressed I called on the LORD and cried out to my God. Out of his temple he listened to my voice; my cry came before him and reached his ears. Then the earth shuddered and rocked; the roots of the mountains trembled and were shaken, because he was furious.

— Psalm 18:2–7

John Calvin · Commentary on the Psalms

...
